article.title: Hennessy VS vs VSOP vs XO: What the Grades Actually Mean
article.body:
Hennessy VS vs VSOP vs XO: What the Grades Actually Mean

The letters are legal age grades for cognac. VS must be aged at least two years in oak, VSOP at least four and XO at least ten, and the minimum applies to the youngest brandy in the blend. Drinks House 247 suggests VS for mixing, VSOP for both mixing and sipping, and XO for drinking neat.

Every bottle of Hennessy carries one of a handful of letter codes, and the price climbs steeply between them. The codes are not marketing labels invented by the house. They are age categories defined for the whole Cognac appellation, and every cognac producer uses the same rules.

What do VS, VSOP and XO stand for?

The abbreviations are English, a legacy of the British merchants who dominated the cognac trade in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

  • VS stands for Very Special. It is sometimes shown as three stars.
  • VSOP stands for Very Superior Old Pale. "Pale" referred to a style without added colour or sweetening, although today it is simply a grade name.
  • XO stands for Extra Old.

The minimum ages, side by side

Cognac is a blend of many eaux-de-vie, the young brandies distilled from white wine and aged in oak. The age on a grade is the age of the youngest eau-de-vie in the blend. Older brandies are almost always included too, so the average age of a bottle is higher than its legal minimum.

Grade Minimum age in oak Typical character Best used for
VS 2 years Fresh, fruity, vanilla and young oak; a noticeable alcohol lift Long drinks and cocktails
VSOP 4 years Rounder and smoother; baking spice, dried apricot, more integrated oak Both mixing and sipping
Napoléon 6 years A step between VSOP and XO in richness Sipping
XO 10 years Dried fruit, candied peel, leather, cocoa and a long, soft finish Drinking neat

The XO minimum was raised from six years to ten in 2018, so older writing that quotes six years is out of date. Hennessy also makes cognacs above XO, such as Paradis, which are blends of very old eaux-de-vie rather than a separate legal grade.

What actually changes with age?

All cognac starts the same way: white wine, mostly from the Ugni Blanc grape, distilled twice in copper pot stills and filled into French oak barrels. What separates a VS from an XO is time in those barrels.

In the first few years, the spirit takes on vanilla and wood tannin quickly and loses its raw edge. Between roughly four and ten years it becomes rounder, the fruit shifts from fresh to dried, and spice notes develop. Beyond ten years, slow oxidation through the wood produces what the Cognac trade calls rancio: a savoury, nutty, slightly mushroomy depth found only in old brandy. Each year in the barrel, a small share of the spirit also evaporates, which is part of why older grades cost so much more.

Which one should you buy?

Buy for how you will drink it, not for the letters.

  • For cocktails and long drinks, VS is the sensible choice. Its fresh fruit and vanilla stand up to ginger ale, tonic or citrus, and an older cognac's subtlety would be lost under a mixer. A cognac and ginger ale over ice is the classic serve.
  • For a bottle that does both, VSOP is the best all-rounder. It works in a Sidecar or an Old Fashioned-style serve, and it is smooth enough to sip with a single ice cube.
  • For drinking neat, XO earns its price. It is built to be sipped slowly, at room temperature, where the complexity has room to show.

An honest note: mixing XO into a cocktail is not wrong, but most of what you pay for disappears. If the bottle is for a party where it will meet a mixer, a VS or VSOP is better value and will taste just as good in the glass.

How should you serve each grade?

  • VS: over plenty of ice with ginger ale or soda and a twist of orange, or in a Sidecar.
  • VSOP: neat or with one ice cube in a tumbler, or as the base of a spirit-forward cocktail.
  • XO: neat, at around 18 to 20°C, in a tulip glass or small snifter. A few drops of water can open the aroma. Let it sit in the glass for a few minutes before drinking.

Avoid warming cognac over a flame or in a heated glass. It drives off the alcohol vapour first and flattens the aroma.

Does cognac improve in the bottle?

No. Unlike wine, cognac stops ageing once it is bottled. A 20-year-old bottle of VS is still a VS. Stored upright, away from light and heat, an unopened bottle keeps indefinitely. Once opened, it stays in good condition for a year or two, gradually losing aroma as the level in the bottle drops and more air is trapped inside.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between Hennessy VS, VSOP and XO?

They are legal age grades. VS is aged at least two years in oak, VSOP at least four and XO at least ten, measured by the youngest brandy in the blend. Older grades are smoother and more complex.

Is Hennessy XO worth the extra money?

For drinking neat, usually yes, because ten or more years in oak brings dried fruit, spice and a long finish. For mixing with ginger ale or in cocktails, VS or VSOP is better value.

How old is Hennessy XO?

Every eau-de-vie in an XO must be at least ten years old. The blend also contains much older brandies, so its average age is higher than the minimum.

Should cognac be served cold?

VS can be served over ice in a long drink. VSOP and XO are best neat or with a single ice cube, at around 18 to 20°C, so the aroma can open.
